title: Early influences: Fletcher, Red Nichols and Lips Page
summary: Roy explains he sounded like Bix and a saxophone, and that Lips Page, meeting him in Oklahoma City, thought he played like a white man; he calls Louis-style playing Southern trumpet.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: So you were listening to Duke then?
No! Except that I had heard, you know. My band was Fletcher's band. That was my band. And Red Nichols' Five Pennies; I liked them.
But that has surprised some people when you've mentioned that. But I guess those records were pretty hip at that time.

Well, I liked them, because those were what I was exposed to. It's a funny thing. The first time Lips Page heard me, he said, "Goddamn, where did this cat come from playing like an ofay, man?" But I was playing like Bix, you know! Things like that. And plus, playing like a saxophone, which put me away from the trumpet, with the split notes and the Louis Armstrong scene, you know, that... So it was a little strange to hear me!
You said you met Lips pretty early.
Yeah, we were in Oklahoma City, playing, of all the theatres, the Eldridge Theatre -- the name of the theatre. I think he was with the Blue Devils then. Yeah, I
think he was with the Blue Devils.
And I guess he was on a Louis kick then, wasn't he?

To me, I called it a Southern trumpet player. The way some of those guys played like that, to me, was like Southern trumpet playing, really because... Well I had never heard nobody play like that, you know. And by that time, I had heard the distinction between the North and the South.
